intro/hello: Show a photo to a three year old and ask what is in it. You get an answer in under a second.
intro/numbers: Show it to a computer, and it receives something far less friendly: a block of a few thousand numbers.
intro/gap: This lecture is about the gap between those two, and about the simplest possible way to bridge it.
intro/simple: The idea: to label a new image, find the most similar image you have already seen, and copy its label.
intro/habits: It beats chance, it fails in instructive ways, and it teaches habits every later chapter relies on: training, validation and test data, hyperparameters, and honest evaluation.
intro/go: Let us start with the task itself.
task/task: Image classification means: given an image, pick one label from a fixed list of categories.
task/built: Plane, car, cat, and so on. It sounds narrow, but finding objects, outlining them, and describing scenes are all built on top of it.
task/grid: To a computer, an image is a grid of pixels.
task/pixel: Each pixel is three numbers: how much red, green and blue light it has.
task/byte: Each is a whole number, from zero for none, to two hundred and fifty five for full. One byte.
task/zoom: Zoom into a patch of the red channel, and this is all that is really there.
task/shape: Thirty two pixels wide, thirty two tall, three colors each: three thousand and seventy two numbers.
task/job: A classifier must turn them into one word. Yet nothing in the numbers says cat. The meaning lives only in how they are arranged.
hard/gap: Recognizing a cat is effortless for you, so it is easy to underestimate. The difficulty has a name: the semantic gap, between raw pixels and the meaning we want.
hard/each: Here are six real cats from the dataset. Each changes the numbers a lot, while the answer stays the same.
hard/view: Viewpoint. Move the camera, and nearly every pixel changes.
hard/scale: Scale. It can fill the frame, or be a few pixels across.
hard/deform: Deformation. Cats stretch, curl up, and sprawl.
hard/occl: Occlusion. Part of it hides behind a window frame.
hard/light: Illumination. In a dark room, only the eyes are left.
hard/clutter: Background clutter. An orange cat, among orange fruit.
hard/intra: And intra class variation: one label, every size, color and breed.
hard/inv: A good classifier must be invariant to all of this, while staying sensitive to what does matter, like a house cat versus a lynx.
hard/rules: Nobody knows how to write that down as rules. Early computer vision tried: find edges, then describe a cat as an arrangement of shapes.
hard/brittle: It was brittle, and every new category meant starting over.
data/learn: So we do what you would do with a child: show lots of examples. Collect labeled images, and let an algorithm learn the look of each class. This is the data driven approach.
data/input: It has three steps. First, the input: a training set of N images, each labeled with one of K classes.
data/training: Second, learning: build a model from them. This is called training.
data/eval: Third, evaluation: have it label new images, the test set, and compare with the true labels. In code, that is two functions: train, and predict.
data/cifar: Our dataset is see-far ten: sixty thousand tiny color images in ten classes, split into fifty thousand for training and ten thousand for testing.
data/sample: From here on, we work with a balanced sample of it: a thousand training images, and two hundred test images.
data/rows: Read along any row, and the challenges show up at once: front and side, near and far, on carpet and on grass.
l1/rule: Now, the simplest classifier there is. Training: memorize every image and its label. Prediction: find the most similar training image, and answer with its label.
l1/number: But most similar has to become a number. The direct way compares two images position by position.
l1/two: Here is a test image, I one, and a training image, I two.
l1/sub: At each of the three thousand and seventy two positions, subtract one number from the other.
l1/abs: Then drop the sign, so minus thirty counts as thirty. That is the absolute value.
l1/pic: The gaps form a third picture: dark where the images agree, bright where they differ.
l1/win: Here are sixteen of them, from one window of the red channel.
l1/sum: Add up every gap, and you get one number: the L one distance. Zero means identical; bigger means more different.
l1/wrap: One trap. Images arrive as unsigned bytes, which cannot go negative: ten minus twenty wraps around to two hundred and forty six.
l1/astype: That silently wrecks every distance, so convert to signed integers first, with as type.
nn/wrap: Wrap that distance in train and predict, and we have a complete classifier.
nn/train: Training just memorizes everything. All the work happens at prediction time, one test image at a time.
nn/broad: Subtract the test image from every row of the training matrix at once. NumPy calls this broadcasting.
nn/axis: Sum along each row, with axis equals one, and you have one distance per training image.
nn/argmin: Find the smallest. Not its value, but its position: that is arg min.
nn/label: The label stored there is the prediction. Here, a cat, which is right.
nn/acc: To score it, compare every guess with the true label. Each comparison is true or false, and their mean is the accuracy.
nn/result: On the full see-far ten, this classifier gets about thirty eight point six percent of the test images right.
nn/compare: Far better than the ten percent of guessing. Far worse than people, at about ninety four, or the convolutional networks of twenty sixteen, at about ninety five.
l2/other: The other common distance is L two: the ordinary, straight line distance.
l2/recipe: Square each difference instead of dropping its sign. Add the squares up, then take the square root.
l2/two: In two dimensions, that is Pythagoras. Go three across and four up. L one walks the grid and gets seven. L two cuts straight across and gets five. Images just have three thousand and seventy two directions instead of two.
l2/squares: The squaring is what sets it apart. A gap of ten counts a hundred, a gap of a hundred counts ten thousand. So L two hates one big difference far more than many small ones.
l2/acc: With the same classifier, L two gets about thirty five point four percent, a little below L one.
l2/real: Here is a real test image, a white cat, with its ten nearest training images by L two.
l2/none: Not one of them is a cat: six planes, three ships and a deer.
l2/why: What they share is a pale blue gray color. Pixel distances see color and layout far more than content.
l2/swap: Switch to L one, and the order shuffles. But the story stays the same.
noloops/slow: Comparing every test image with every training image, pair by pair, is slow in Python. Assignment one asks for it with no loops at all.
noloops/expand: The trick is school algebra: A minus B, squared, equals A squared, plus B squared, minus two A B. Summed over every position, a distance splits into three parts.
noloops/own: Each image's own sum of squares: one per test image, and one per training image.
noloops/cross: And the cross term, a dot product. For every pair at once, those form one matrix product, which NumPy hands to a heavily optimized library.
noloops/broad: Broadcasting adds a column to a row to fill the whole table. Typically, that is a hundred times faster than two nested loops, or more.
knn/fragile: Copying the label of the single closest image is fragile.
knn/odd: If that one image is odd, say mislabeled, or a cat on a blue blanket like a ship on water, the answer is wrong.
knn/vote: So ask more neighbors. k nearest neighbors finds the k closest training images, and lets them vote.
knn/win: The most common label wins. With k equal to one, it is nearest neighbor again.
knn/plane: In two dimensions, we can watch it. Color every spot of the plane by the label it would get. These are decision regions, and their borders, decision boundaries.
knn/islands: At k equals one, every point claims the area nearest to it, so these three outliers carve out islands of the wrong color.
knn/five: Raise k to five, and they are outvoted. The islands vanish, and the boundaries smooth out.
knn/ties: Blank patches are ties, where no class has a majority.
knn/metric: The distance matters too. At k equals one under L one, every boundary runs across, up and down, or on a diagonal.
knn/howbig: In practice you want k above one. But how far? Too large, and small classes get outvoted. You cannot settle that by thinking.
validation/hyper: K is a hyperparameter: a setting of the learning algorithm itself, as opposed to something learned from the data.
validation/hypername: Hyper, as in above: it sits one level above the parameters. You choose it; training chooses the parameters.
validation/more: The distance is another. You rarely know good values in advance, so you try several, and keep what works best.
validation/onwhat: But best on what? The tempting answer is the test set, and it is a serious mistake.
validation/tuned: Keep whichever k scores best on the test set, and you have quietly tuned to those test images. The number you report is now too optimistic.
validation/exam: Treat the test set like a sealed exam. Make every choice without it, then open it exactly once, at the end.
validation/carve: Instead, carve a validation set out of the training data: of fifty thousand images, train on forty nine thousand, and hold back one thousand.
validation/loop: Train with each candidate k, score it on the validation images, and keep the best.
validation/practice: It is a practice test you may look at as often as you like.
crossval/noisy: With little data, one validation set is a noisy judge: a few lucky images can make one k look better than it is.
crossval/folds: Cross validation buys a steadier verdict with more computation. Split the training data into five equal folds.
crossval/rotate: Train on four, and validate on the fifth. Then rotate, so every fold takes one turn as validation.
crossval/avg: Average the five scores. Every image validates once, and trains four times.
crossval/run: Here it is on our thousand training images, with L one. Each faint dot is one fold. The line is their average, and the bars show how much the folds disagree.
crossval/flat: With so few images, the curve is low and nearly flat, and the folds disagree by several points. Exactly when averaging earns its keep.
crossval/best: The best average is at k equals five. On the full see-far ten, the course notes found about seven.
crossval/test: Only now, once, the test set: thirty one percent. That is the number to report.
crossval/practice: Folds multiply the cost of every experiment, so with big datasets and slow networks, people use one split, training on half to ninety percent of the data.
limits/pros: A verdict. Nearest neighbors is simple, and takes no time to train. It pays at prediction, comparing each image with every stored one.
limits/backwards: That is backwards. Training happens once, and may take days. Prediction happens every time, often on a phone, and must be fast.
limits/ann: Approximate search libraries, such as flan, help a lot. But they cannot fix a deeper problem.
limits/deeper: Pixel distances ask whether two images have similar colors in the same places. That is only loosely tied to what they show.
limits/edits: Take this dog, and make three edits that keep it a dog. Shift it four pixels. Dim it to sixty percent. Black out its middle.
limits/frog: Now find the closest image of another class. A frog, on a white background, just like the dog.
limits/bars: Measure the L two distance from the dog to each. Every edited copy is farther away than the frog.
limits/fluke: No fluke: across our thousand images, a four pixel shift lands farther than the nearest other class almost half the time.
limits/tsne: Lay the dataset out with tee snee, so images close in L two sit together, and neighbors share backgrounds far more often than a class.
curse/size: There is also a problem of size. Nearest neighbors needs examples that cover the space densely, so every new image has a similar one nearby.
curse/line: A line, with one example every tenth of the way, needs ten. A square needs a hundred. A cube, a thousand. Each dimension multiplies the bill by ten.
curse/pixels: An image has three thousand and seventy two dimensions. Ten to that power has three thousand and seventy three digits. No dataset comes close.
curse/strange: And something stranger. Scatter five hundred random points in a cube, and measure their distances to one more.
curse/two: In two dimensions, the distances spread out. Some points really are near, others really far.
curse/up: Now raise the number of dimensions. Ten. A hundred. A thousand.
curse/spike: The distances bunch into a narrow spike. The nearest point is barely closer than the farthest, and nearest loses its meaning.
curse/real: Real images are not random, which is why nearest neighbors beats chance at all. But every method on raw pixels fights this bunching.
closing/practice: If you do use K N N, on good features rather than raw pixels, here is the recipe.
closing/pre: Normalize each feature to zero mean and unit variance, and reduce the dimensions if there are many, for example with P C A.
closing/tune: Tune k and the distance on validation data. Switch to approximate search if it is slow. Then test once, and report that number.
closing/recap: To recap. Image classification turns three thousand and seventy two numbers into one label, across a wide semantic gap, by learning from examples instead of rules.
closing/recap2: K N N lets the k most similar training images vote. It trains instantly, predicts slowly, and its pixel distances track color more than content. Hyperparameters are tuned on validation data, never the test set.
closing/next: The next chapter flips the trade. A linear classifier distills the training set into one template per class, and throws the images away. Prediction becomes a single matrix multiply.
